text:
**Donald Knuth** is a pioneering computer scientist born in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, of Midwestern Lutheran German heritage. Early on, he demonstrated extraordinary problem-solving skills, notably winning a word-rearrangement contest in eighth grade by systematically using an unabridged dictionary. Knuth earned scholarships and degrees at Case Institute of Technology, initially majoring in physics, then switching to mathematics. He was introduced to computers via the IBM 650 and demonstrated early proficiency by rewriting assembly and compiler code. After earning a PhD in mathematics at Caltech under Marshall Hall, he joined Caltech's faculty, consulted for Burroughs Corporation, and developed compilers and simulation languages. Knuth authored *The Art of Computer Programming* beginning in 1968, originally intending a single book but expanding it into a multi-volume foundational work on algorithm analysis.
In 1969, Knuth joined Stanford University, eventually becoming Fletcher Jones Professor of Computer Science and later Professor Emeritus of The Art of Computer Programming. His work spans publications on algorithms, programming languages, and digital typesetting. He created TeX and Metafont to address digital typography challenges and invented literate programming as a methodology to write programs as readable literature. Knuth is also known for his engaging humor, such as paying bounties for typographical errors in his books. Married to Nancy Jill Carter since 1961, they have two children, and Knuth is also an accomplished organist and composer. His honors include the first ACM Grace Murray Hopper Award (1971), Turing Award (1974), National Medal of Science (1979), and Kyoto Prize (1996), among others. He is known by the Chinese name Gao Dena and remains a towering figure in computer science and mathematics.
